items.name: bulk-paste-field
items.title: Bulk paste field
items.description: Paste a list of emails, SKUs or URLs and see what was understood: valid, invalid and duplicate counts, the bad lines listed, and one-click tidying.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak the text, one item per line; onItemsChange speaks the clean list (normalised, valid, each once, in order, up to max) after a pause in the typing and whenever a tidy action changes it. validate gets the normalised line and returns true or nothing when it is fine, false for the default reason, or the reason in words; normalise decides what a line is for the duplicate check and the list (trim and lower-case an address, upper-case a SKU), and by default only trims. Under the field a summary reads 38 valid, 2 invalid, 5 duplicates in a polite live region that is worked out once the typing pauses, never on every key, together with the panel and the marks beside the line numbers; the check is one pass with a Set, so ten thousand lines take a few milliseconds. The lines that need attention (invalid ones and, with max, the lines past the limit) are listed in a compact panel, five at a time with a Show more, each a button that selects the line and scrolls it into view. Remove duplicates, Remove invalid and, with max, Keep the first N each rewrite the text in one click, keep every other line in order, and offer Undo. A paste that holds commas, semicolons or tabs becomes one item per line through the browser's own insertText, so the text keeps its undo history; a plain column pastes as it is. The line numbers are drawn only for the lines in view, with fixed pixel metrics, so they follow the scrolling and stay on their lines. It is a plain textarea, so it stays fast with thousands of lines. A change to validate or normalise is picked up on the next edit. name goes on the textarea, rows sets how many lines are visible, label and hideLabel name the field, and labels renames every phrase.

items.name: quick-phrases-field
items.title: Quick phrases field
items.description: A textarea with one-tap phrases underneath, such as Leave at the door or Ring twice: tap to add, tap again to take it out, typing stays free.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak the whole text as a plain string; defaultValue starts it uncontrolled. phrases is a list of strings or { id, text } (use ids when the same words appear twice or the text is translated). A tap adds the phrase behind the text after separator (a line break by default, or ", ", ". " or " " to keep one sentence going, or two line breaks to keep paragraphs apart, where taking a phrase out takes its gap with it; a phrase that ends its own sentence with a full stop, exclamation mark or question mark is not given a second full stop), and a second tap takes it out again together with its separator. A long phrase wraps inside its chip instead of being cut off, and on a touch screen the chips are taller so a thumb can hit them. A phrase counts as present when it stands as a piece of its own between the separators, whatever the capitals and with or without a closing full stop, so typing it by hand presses its chip too. maxLength is the textarea's own limit and also disables any chip that would not fit, with a line under the chips saying how many need more room than is left; a chip that is already in the text can always be removed. Every add and remove is announced politely (Added Leave at the door). label names the field (hideLabel keeps it for assistive technology), phrasesLabel renames the small heading over the chips, name posts the text, and labels renames the announcements and the lines about the limit. The pure helpers addPhrase, removePhrase and locate live in quick-phrases-field/phrases.

items.name: number-range-field
items.title: Number range field
items.description: From and To fields for filters: either end can stay open, an end below the start is explained in words, and one unit sits beside both.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { min, max } where an open end is null. A range whose end is below its start is never reported: it is explained in words when a field is left (The maximum cannot be below the minimum of 60,000 km) and the later field carries aria-invalid until it is right. min and max bound both ends (typing outside them is brought in when the field is left, with a line saying so), step is what an arrow key adds and Shift makes ten times as much, and the arrow keys never take the end below the start. Home and End go to the limits. unit is shown at the end of both fields, label is the legend of the group, locale writes the numbers and decides what a lone comma or point means (1,500 is fifteen hundred where a comma groups; digits of any script, such as Arabic-Indic, Bengali or Devanagari, are understood when typing), grouping=false drops the thousands separator for numbers that are not amounts, such as a year, name posts <name>-min and <name>-max, and labels renames every phrase including the No min and No max placeholders. The two ends sit side by side while the group is wide enough for a number and its unit in each, and stack in a column (with a small to between them) when the group itself is narrower, the sooner the longer the unit is, which is a matter of the group's width and not of the screen's, so a card on a phone does not clip a number. The fields are spinbuttons that read their value with the unit.

items.name: number-range-field-demo
items.title: Number range field demo
items.description: A working preview of Number range field.

items.name: code-field
items.title: Code field
items.description: A monospace field for JSON, CSS or a webhook body: line numbers, Tab indents, Escape then Tab leaves, and JSON mistakes are named by line.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak the text. Tab indents (to the next tab stop, or every line the selection touches), Shift+Tab takes one level off, Enter keeps the indentation and goes one level deeper behind a bracket, all through the browser's own editing so undo still works. Escape followed by Tab leaves the field, so a keyboard user is never trapped, and a visible hint says so. language="json" checks the text after a pause with a parser of its own, so the message is the same in every browser: Unexpected token } at line 4, column 3, Trailing comma before }, Missing comma, single quotes, comments, an unclosed bracket, and a character nobody can see is named (Unexpected non-breaking space, Unexpected byte order mark). The line is marked in the gutter and across the text, Go to line jumps to it, and onValidate receives { valid: true, empty } or { valid: false, message, line, column, offset } each time a check settles. The Format button pretty-prints valid JSON at token level, so numbers keep every digit and keys keep their order. language="plain" is for CSS or any other text. rows sets the visible lines, readOnly drops the editing keys and the hint, name posts the text, and a label is paired by id. labels renames every word the field says (Format, Valid JSON, the hint, the status row); the messages that name a mistake come from the checker and are in English. validateJson and formatJson live in code-field/json.

items.name: code-field-demo
items.title: Code field demo
items.description: A working preview of Code field.

items.name: variable-textarea
items.title: Variable textarea
items.description: A template box with an Insert variable menu: pick first_name and the token lands at the caret, with a preview that fills in sample data.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak the raw template, always, also while the preview is showing. variables is a list of { key, label, sample }, where a key is letters of any script, digits, underscores, dots and hyphens (no spaces); delimiters is the pair around a key (["{{", "}}"] by default, ["%", "%"] works too). Insert variable opens the house dropdown with each label, its token and its sample; choosing one puts the token where the caret was, in place of any selection (at the end if the text never had the focus), through the browser's own editing so undo takes it out, and returns the focus to the text. The Preview toggle (preview, defaultPreview and onPreviewChange when you want to drive it) swaps the text for the same message with every sample filled in. A variable that is written but was not passed is flagged in words ({{frist_name}} is not a variable) with the nearest real one offered, and the text carries aria-invalid. maxLength limits the raw template and disables a variable that no longer fits, saying how many characters it needs. labels renames every phrase, the name the text has for a screen reader included. parseTemplate and fillTemplate live in variable-textarea/tokens.

items.name: variable-textarea-demo
items.title: Variable textarea demo
items.description: A working preview of Variable textarea.

items.name: sms-message-field
items.title: SMS message field
items.description: A text message box that counts messages, not characters, and names the emoji or curly quote that turns one message into several.
items.docs: value and onValueChange(value, count) speak the message and what it costs. One message holds 160 characters in the standard GSM alphabet and 70 as soon as one character is outside it; a text that is split holds 153 or 67 per part. Characters of the extension table (€ [ ] { } ~ ^ \ |) and emoji take two places, and a character is never split over two parts. The counter reads 2 messages, 214 characters, Unicode beside a bar with one segment per message, and a line names what forced Unicode (an emoji, a curly apostrophe) so it can be taken out, and adds that emoji count as two characters each while one is in the text; Use plain characters swaps curly quotes, dashes, the ellipsis and special spaces for the standard ones through the browser's own editing, so undo brings them back. maxSegments is a soft limit: past it the counter, the bar and aria-invalid turn to the error colour and nothing is cut off. senderLabel is shown beside the label and is not counted. The number of messages is announced politely, only when it changes. countSms, plainText and the alphabet tables live in sms-message-field/sms.

items.title: SMS message field demo
items.description: A working preview of SMS message field.

items.name: limit-field
items.title: Limit field
items.description: A number that can also be no limit: a switch for Unlimited that reveals the number field, for usage limits, seats and quotas.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak a number, or null for no limit; defaultValue null starts unlimited. Turning the switch on brings back the last number (defaultLimit, 100, the first time) and moves the focus into the number field; turning it off reports null and keeps the number for next time. min defaults to 1, because a limit of 0 would be no use, and max bounds the number. unit is a word shown behind the number, or { one, other } to follow the number (1 seat, 10 seats) with locale choosing the plural. offLabel is what the field says while it is unlimited. The switch controls the number, and the number is named after the switch and read with its unit (Usage limit, 100 uses). name posts the number, or an empty value while it is unlimited. id, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, aria-label and aria-labelledby go to the number, so a form label and an error line can be wired to it; aria-invalid gives it the error border.

items.name: limit-field-demo

items.description: A working preview of Limit field.

items.name: filename-field
items.title: File name field
items.description: Rename a file without breaking it: the name is editable, the extension stays fixed beside it and forbidden characters are explained.
items.docs: value and onValueChange(name, { valid }) speak the whole name, extension included. The input holds the name only; the extension sits behind it as a fixed part of the field (.tar.gz and its kin stay together) and is put back on the reported name. Focusing the field selects the name. Characters a file name cannot hold (/ \ : * ? " < > | and control characters) are refused with the reason in words (Names cannot contain a slash (/)), spaces at the start are dropped and spaces at the end are trimmed when the field is left, and typing or pasting the extension again is caught. taken lists the names that exist; a match (capitals ignored) is flagged with aria-invalid and the next free name is offered (Use report (2).pdf). maxLength counts the whole name. extensionEditable gives the extension a box of its own and warns while it differs from the one it started with. The box stays whatever it holds: it is sized to its text, a lone dot is kept while it has the focus (so deleting an extension down to its dot does not empty it), and an empty box shows its .ext placeholder, so an extension can be typed back or added to a name that had none. name posts the whole name in a hidden input, labels renames every phrase.

items.name: filename-field-demo
items.title: File name field demo
items.description: A working preview of File name field.

items.name: image-url-field
items.title: Image URL field
items.description: Paste an image address and see it load: a live thumbnail, a clear failed state and optional https-only, with no server call.
items.docs: value and onValueChange(url, { status, width, height }) speak the address. The thumbnail is a plain image element in the field, so no script fetches anything and no server is involved; the request carries referrerPolicy no-referrer and the thumbnail has an empty alt because the label names the field. status is empty, loading, loaded (with the natural size in pixels), failed (That address did not load as an image, also after 15 seconds without an answer) or invalid, an address turned down before any request: not an address, http:// when requireHttps is on, a data: address unless allowData is on, and any scheme other than https, http and data:image. onValueChange is called on every change and again whenever what is known changes: when the image has answered, and when the address comes from outside. debounce (500 ms) keeps half an address from being requested while someone types; a pasted address, or one set from outside, loads at once. The status line is a polite live region, labels renames every phrase, and name posts the address.

items.name: image-url-field-demo
items.title: Image URL field demo
items.description: A working preview of Image URL field.

items.name: color-area-picker
items.title: Color area picker
items.description: Any colour, not just swatches: a saturation and brightness area, a hue slider, optional alpha and a typed code, all keyboard operable.
items.docs: value and onValueChange(value, color) speak the colour as a string in format (hex #2563eb, rgb(37, 99, 235) or hsl(221, 83%, 53%); with alpha the code carries it: eight hex digits, rgba() or hsla()) and as { h, s, v, a } (hue in degrees, saturation and brightness in percent, alpha 0 to 1). value takes a string in any of those formats or the object, and the picker keeps its own hue, so dragging into black, white or grey does not lose it the way a code would. The area is a two-axis slider: arrow keys move 1%, Shift 10%, Home and End go to the left and right edge, Page Up and Page Down to the top and bottom, and its value text reads Saturation 80%, brightness 60%. The hue and opacity sliders are Radix sliders over a rainbow and a quiet checkerboard. The code box accepts #rgb, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa, rgb() and hsl() whatever the format and says what is wrong in words. The chosen colour is shown beside its code with its contrast against white and black in words (4.6:1, passes AA). swatches is a row of presets (a radio group), inline puts the picker in the page instead of behind a button, and the eye dropper button appears only where the browser has one, inside the code box so the code has the whole row (an rgba() or hsla() code keeps its alpha in view, and on the narrowest phone the colour tile beside the box gives way to it). The button shows the code on one line. id, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, aria-label and aria-labelledby go to the button, or to the area when the picker is inline, so a form label and error can be wired to it. name posts the colour. The colour helpers (parseColor, formatColor, contrastRatio) live in color-area-picker/colors.

items.name: week-picker
items.title: Week picker
items.description: Pick a whole week for timesheets and reports: Week 43 with its dates, arrows to step, and a grid where a click on any day takes the row.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { start, end, week, year } with ISO dates; only value.start is read, and week counts in its own year (2025-12-29 is week 1 of 2026). numbering is iso (Monday start) or us (Sunday start). Without now the browser's clock is read, so the server renders no today marker.

items.title: Dimensions field
items.description: Width by height in one field, with a lock that keeps the aspect ratio: change either side and the other follows the ratio set when you locked it.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { width, height, locked }; a size is a number between min (1) and max, or null while its field is empty. The lock keeps the ratio the sizes had when it went on, so rounding never drifts. name adds hidden inputs <name>-width and <name>-height.

items.title: Height field
items.description: A height in centimetres or in feet and inches, with a unit switch that converts what is typed and always reports one number in centimetres.

Switching never changes the stored height.

items.description: Type 250k, 1.2M or 3b and it understands: a number field that reads shorthand, shows the full figure under it and reports a plain number.

It commits on Enter or when the field is left, never while typing. 1,2k and 1.2k both read as 1200.

items.title: Natural date field
items.description: Type a date the way you would say it, such as tomorrow, next friday or in 3 weeks, and see the date it was understood as before you commit.

Pass now and timeZone so tomorrow is the same day on the server and in the browser. The calendar button's Calendar reads the browser's own clock. parseNaturalDate is the parser as a function.

items.name: wheel-picker
items.title: Wheel picker
items.description: Scrolling columns that snap to a value, for times, durations and numbers on a phone: swipe, tap or use the arrow keys.
items.docs: columns is a list of { id, options, loop, label }, and wheelRange(from, to, { step, pad }) from wheel-picker/wheel writes numbers as options. value and onValueChange speak an array with the chosen value of every column, reported when a swipe comes to rest. It draws no surface of its own: put it on a card, or in a Drawer.

items.name: currency-exchange-field
items.title: Currency exchange field
items.description: You send, they get: two linked amounts in two currencies tied together by the rates you supply, so editing either side updates the other.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { send, receive, fixed }: each side is { minor, currency } in minor units (1250 is 12.50 in euros and 1,250 in yen) and fixed is the side typed last. rates is a table or a function (from, to) => rate. min, max and fee.flat are minor units of the currency sent, so pass one figure per currency code when several can be sent.

items.name: time-estimate-field
items.title: Time estimate field
items.description: Type 1h 30m, 90m or 1.5h and it understands: a text field that parses durations the way task trackers do and shows what it read.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak minutes, or null when the field was emptied or could not be read; the second argument says whether it is inside max, and a longer estimate is still reported. It commits on Enter or when the field is left and rewrites the text as 1h 30m. A day is hoursPerDay hours (8) and a week daysPerWeek days (5).

items.name: time-estimate-field-demo
items.title: Time estimate field demo
items.description: A working preview of Time estimate field.

items.name: cron-field
items.title: Cron field
items.description: A cron field that explains itself: type 0 9 * * 1-5 and read “At 09:00, Monday to Friday”, with the next runs listed in your time zone.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak the expression as typed, with { valid } as a second argument: valid is true once the expression is complete and every field is right. A cron expression has five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and the parser reads * and ?, numbers, lists (1,15), ranges (1-5), steps (*/15 and 10-40/10), JAN to DEC and SUN to SAT, the @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly and @yearly shortcuts, and 7 as Sunday. Under the input the five fields are drawn apart so the reading can be seen, and a sentence says what the expression does in plain English. The sentence is English whatever the locale, the names of the days and months included, so it never mixes two languages; locale decides whether the clock is written on 12 or 24 hours (in the sentence and in the menu of schedules) and how the dates and the distances in the list of runs are written, and a locale that is not a language tag, such as en_US, is read as en-US. Where a schedule runs in bursts it says so (Every 15 minutes during every 2nd hour) and a window runs from the first run to the last (from 09:00 to 17:45). A field that is wrong is named in words (Minute must be 0 to 59) and marked in the drawing, but only once its word is finished: while the caret is still in the last word nothing is flagged, and a field that is not focused is always judged. timeZone sets the clock the schedule follows (an IANA name, default UTC) and the next runs, count of them (default 3), are worked out and written on it, each with how far away it is (in 15 minutes, in 6 hr 15 min, tomorrow, in 3 days). A time that daylight saving skips is left out and a time that happens twice is listed once. now fixes the moment the runs are counted from (a Date, a timestamp or an ISO string); without it the browser's clock is read after mount and again every half minute, so the server and the browser never disagree. presets replaces the menu of six schedules ({ label, value }[]) or turns it off with false. Like the other fields it never blocks a submit; the parser, describeCron and nextRuns are plain functions in cron-field/cron, for a server to check an expression with the same rules.

items.title: Cron field demo
items.description: A working preview of Cron field.

items.name: barcode-field
items.title: Barcode field
items.description: EAN-13, UPC-A and EAN-8 numbers grouped as printed on the pack, with the check digit verified and a missing one added in a tap.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { digits, format, valid }: digits are the digits without spaces, format is ean13, upca or ean8 (null while a number in auto is too short to tell) and valid is true when the number is complete and its GS1 check digit is right. The text is written in groups as it is printed, 4 006381 333931 for an EAN-13, 0 36000 29145 2 for a UPC-A and 7351 3537 for an EAN-8, however it is typed or pasted (spaces, hyphens and letters are dropped, and an extra zero in front of a pasted GTIN-14 is dropped too), and the caret stays after the same digit. format fixes one format, or auto (the default) reads it from the length: 13 digits is an EAN-13, 12 a UPC-A, 8 an EAN-8. While the field is in use, twelve digits that are a right UPC-A are not called finished, since they may be the front of an EAN-13: the line stays neutral (Valid as a UPC-A. Typing an EAN-13? One more digit.), the check mark waits until the field is left and Add check digit offers the one the EAN-13 asks for. A wrong last digit is said at once and says what it should have been; a number one digit short offers the check digit it asks for as a button (Add check digit 1); a number that is still short is only called wrong once the field has been left. The line under the field says which format was read and how far along the number is. trailing takes something of your own at the end of the field, such as a Scan button. name adds a hidden input with the digits, id lands on the input, and required, disabled and placeholder work as on any input. checkDigit, isValidBarcode, groupBarcode and readBarcode are plain functions in barcode-field/gs1, for the server.

items.name: barcode-field-demo
items.title: Barcode field demo
items.description: A working preview of Barcode field.

items.name: national-id-field
items.title: National ID field
items.description: A personal identity number per country, such as a Dutch BSN or a US SSN, formatted as printed and checked with its own checksum, masked by default.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak the number without separators and { valid, country }: valid is true when the number is complete and passes its country's checks. country and onCountryChange choose the country by ISO code (defaultCountry when you do not control it); the menu comes with Belgium, Canada, Germany, Spain, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Sweden and the United States, each with its own arithmetic (the Dutch eleven test, the Luhn digit, the Spanish check letter, the Italian check character, the areas of a Social Security number that are never issued), and countries adds a country or replaces one with a rule of your own { name, label, describe, example, maxLength, keyboard, clean, format, check, messages }. The number is written as it is printed (111 222 333, 123-45-6789, AB 12 34 56 C) and only the characters of that country are accepted. A wrong number is explained in words (A BSN has nine digits and passes the eleven test) once the field has been left, or at once when the number is as long as it gets, and the words never repeat the number, so nothing is read out, logged or kept. With masked (the default) the number is hidden behind dots as soon as the field is left and a button, named Show number, shows it again; masked={false} keeps it in view. autoComplete is off and password managers are told to ignore the field. name adds a hidden input with the number and <name>-country with the country; id lands on the number input. The checks are arithmetic only, so they catch a typo, not a number that was never issued. checkNationalId, isNationalId, formatNationalId and the table itself are plain functions in national-id-field/ids.

items.name: national-id-field-demo
items.title: National ID field demo
items.description: A working preview of National ID field.

items.name: password-generator
items.title: Password generator
items.description: Make a strong password or passphrase on demand: length, character sets, copy and regenerate, using the browser's secure random source.
items.docs: onUse is called with the password when Use this password is pressed; the button is only there when you give it. defaultMode is password or passphrase and defaultLength the length it starts at: characters for a password (12 to 64, default 20) and words for a passphrase (3 to 8, default 6). A password is made from the length, the numbers and symbols switches and Avoid look-alikes (I l 1 | O 0 o), and every set that is on is used at least once; a passphrase is words drawn from wordlist (default: over a thousand everyday words, about ten bits each, and the estimate follows the list you give) with a capital on each and, if you like, one digit. Every character and every word comes from crypto.getRandomValues through rejection sampling, so none is likelier than another, and nothing is sent, stored or logged; where the browser has no secure random source the field says so instead of making a weak password. Nothing is made while rendering, so the server never produces a password: it appears as soon as the page is on screen. The strength is stated as bits, a word (Weak, Fair, Strong, Very strong) and a sentence from the entropy and a billion guesses a second (Would take centuries at a billion guesses a second). Digits are drawn in weight and symbols in a lighter tone so look-alikes are easy to tell apart. Each new result is announced once, politely, without reading the password aloud. The box keeps its height from one result to the next, so Regenerate and Copy stay under the pointer: a password is broken at any character, so a length always takes the same lines, and a passphrase keeps room for words of a typical length. label names the result for a screen reader (default Generated password), and locale writes the numbers (a tag that is not a language tag, such as en_US, is read as en-US). It needs nothing from a Password input, so it also serves an admin screen that sets a temporary password. secureRandom, generatePassword, generatePassphrase, passwordEntropy and guessTime are plain functions in password-generator/generate.

items.name: password-generator-demo
items.title: Password generator demo
items.description: A working preview of Password generator.

items.name: rating-breakdown-field
items.title: Rating breakdown field
items.description: Rate several things at once, such as Cleanliness, Location and Value, with stars per row, a Not applicable option and the overall average.
items.docs: aspects is the list of rows, { id, label, description, required }[]. value and onValueChange speak every answer by the id of its row: a number from 1 to max is a rating, null is Not applicable, and a row that is missing has not been answered; onValueChange gets the whole record. The group is a fieldset named by label (description adds a line under it that says what to do), and each row is a group a screen reader announces by name (Cleanliness, 4 stars); it keeps one tab stop and the arrow keys change the stars. Ticking Not applicable switches the row's stars off and drops its rating. The overall score is the mean of the rows that have a rating, shown with one decimal (locale writes it; a tag that is not a language tag, such as en_US, is read as en-US) and partial stars; until every required row has an answer, where an answer is a rating or Not applicable, it says how many rows are rated (3 of 5 rated) and which are still needed instead of showing a number. Optional rows are marked Optional once at least one row is required, on the page and in the name a screen reader reads. showOverall hides the panel, max sets the number of stars (default 5), and name adds the answers to a plain form submit as <name>-<id>: the rating, or na for Not applicable. A change to the overall score is told to a screen reader once the rating has stopped changing. summarizeRatings and averageRating are plain functions in rating-breakdown-field/ratings.

items.title: Rating breakdown field demo
items.description: A working preview of Rating breakdown field.

items.name: aspect-ratio-picker
items.title: Aspect ratio picker
items.description: Choose a crop shape from drawn outlines (1:1, 4:3, 16:9, 9:16) or enter your own ratio, as a radio group.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { width, height } in lowest terms, such as { width: 16, height: 9 }; any size is read as its ratio, so 1920 by 1080 is 16 by 9. ratios is the list on offer, drawn in that order and each at its true proportion with the ratio under it (default 1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9 and 9:16). It is a radio group: the arrow keys move and choose, Tab leaves the group, and the chosen outline is filled and checked. allowCustom (the default) adds a last option, Custom, that opens a width and a height; whatever is typed is reduced and reported, a line says what it reduces to, and the outline of Custom is drawn with it. Where the picker is narrower than 22rem the plus and minus buttons of the two numbers give way, so a number of five digits keeps its room (the arrow keys and typing still work), and below 12rem the numbers stack. A short last row of shapes is stretched to the edge so no cell is left empty, and a shape too thin to hold a check mark is only filled. A value that is not on offer opens Custom by itself. orientationToggle adds a switch that turns every shape on its side; the list is then read as landscape shapes, so 16:9 and 9:16 are one and the same option, and the value turns with the switch. name adds a hidden input with the ratio as 16:9, label names the group for a screen reader, and disabled turns the whole picker off. reduceRatio, sameRatio, flipRatio and ratioLabel are plain functions in aspect-ratio-picker/ratios.

items.name: aspect-ratio-picker-demo
items.title: Aspect ratio picker demo
items.description: A working preview of Aspect ratio picker.

items.name: position-picker
items.title: Position picker
items.description: A 3 by 3 grid to pick where something sits, such as an image anchor, a watermark corner or the position of a toast.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak one of top-left, top-center, top-right, center-left, center, center-right, bottom-left, bottom-center and bottom-right. The nine places sit in a thin frame that reads as a small version of the surface, each dot toward its own edge or corner; the chosen place is a filled dot and the others are hollow. It is a radio group in two dimensions: the arrow keys move along the row and down the column, going round the edge, Home and End jump to the first and last place, and places that cannot be chosen are passed over. positions limits the choice to a subset (CORNERS, exported from position-picker/positions, is the four corners); the others are drawn as faint dots and cannot be reached. The group is named with the choice in words (Watermark position: Top right), label names what is being placed, and the choice is also shown under the frame unless showValue is false. size is sm, default or lg, name adds a hidden input with the place, and disabled turns the picker off. movePosition, positionLabel, POSITIONS and CORNERS are plain helpers in position-picker/positions.

items.name: position-picker-demo
items.title: Position picker demo
items.description: A working preview of Position picker.

items.name: contrast-pair-field
items.title: Contrast pair field
items.description: Choose a text colour and a background and see the contrast ratio with AA and AAA verdicts in words, before the pair ships.
items.docs: value and onValueChange speak { foreground, background } and, going out, the ratio too: onValueChange gets { foreground, background, ratio } with the ratio from 1 to 21. Colours are #rrggbb (#rgb is read as well). Two colour pickers, Text and Background, share the swatches you give (swatches); a Swap button trades the two colours and says so. Where the field is narrower than 17.5rem the two pickers stack, Text above Background, and the Swap button turns to point up and down. Below them a sample is set in the pair, a large line (24px) and a normal one (16px), both of which you can change with sample. The ratio is written large in tabular figures (4.8:1) to two decimals, as the browsers' tools write it, but never rounded up to a number it does not reach: 4.499 is 4.49, not 4.5. Four checks are answered in words, each with an icon and a word and never by colour alone: Normal text AA (4.5:1) and AAA (7:1), Large text AA (3:1) and AAA (4.5:1). The verdicts are told to a screen reader once the colours stop changing. name adds hidden inputs <name>-foreground and <name>-background, and label names the group for a screen reader. normalizeHex, relativeLuminance, contrastRatio, formatRatio and contrastVerdicts are plain functions in contrast-pair-field/contrast, for a build step or a server.

items.name: contrast-pair-field-demo
items.title: Contrast pair field demo
items.description: A working preview of Contrast pair field.

items.name: font-family-select
items.title: Font family select
items.description: Choose a typeface from a list where every font is set in its own face, with a live sample that previews the highlighted one.
items.docs: fonts is a list of { family, stack, label?, group? }: stack is the CSS font-family list the font is drawn with and the value the field reports, so a font that is not there still draws as the next family in its list. The field never loads a font. It draws each name in its own stack and asks the browser which fonts it can draw (a web font that finishes loading is noticed), marks the ones it cannot with 'Not loaded', and says in words which font the sample falls back to. The list opens under the sample, so the sample is never covered: it follows the highlighted font while the list is open, and Escape closes the list and puts it back on the chosen font. Nothing above the list changes height with the font on show: the sample box is always sampleLines tall (2 lines by default, 3 in a field narrower than about 17rem, and a longer sample ends in an ellipsis) and the line that says a font is not loaded keeps its row while any font in the list is missing, so the list never moves under the pointer or the arrow keys. groups sets the order of the headings, recent takes the stacks to pin under Recent (without it the field remembers what was chosen since it appeared), and a screen reader hears each font's name and group. messages replaces the words.

items.name: font-family-select-demo
items.title: Font family select demo
items.description: A working preview of Font family select.

items.name: font-size-field
items.title: Font size field
items.description: A font size you can type, step or pick: minus, a number with its unit and plus, joined to a menu of common sizes, the way editors draw it.
items.docs: value is a number in unit, and sizes is the ladder the list shows and the arrow keys walk: from 16 the up arrow goes to 18, not to 17. Shift with an arrow adds or takes away one step, Alt with the down arrow opens the list, and Enter or leaving the field checks what was typed and brings it into min and max. The number is a spin button read as 'Font size, 16 pixels'. The minus, plus and list buttons are not tab stops, so the whole control is one stop in a toolbar, and they announce the size they set.

items.name: font-size-field-demo
items.title: Font size field demo
items.description: A working preview of Font size field.

items.name: angle-field
items.title: Angle field
items.description: A rotation in degrees as a dial and a number box: drag the handle, type a value or step with the arrow keys, with an optional compass reading.
items.docs: 0 is straight up and the angle grows clockwise, as in CSS, so the value drops into a gradient, a shadow direction or a rotate(). Drag the dial (Shift snaps to snap, 15 degrees by default), press the arrow keys (Shift jumps along the grid, Home goes to 0), or type in the box. With wrap on, the default, past 359 comes 0; with wrap off the angle stops at min and max. The dial is a slider that reads '90 degrees', or with compass '90 degrees, east', and size is sm, default or lg.

items.name: angle-field-demo
items.title: Angle field demo
items.description: A working preview of Angle field.

items.name: box-sides-field
items.title: Box sides field
items.description: Edit padding or margin on four sides: a small box with a number on each edge and a link in the middle that moves all four at once.
items.docs: value is { top, right, bottom, left } and onValueChange is also told whether the sides are linked. With the link on, changing one side sets all four. sides={2} shows a vertical and a horizontal field and mirrors them on the other two edges. The sides are checked as they are typed, the arrow keys step the side the cursor is in (Shift for ten steps), and Tab goes clockwise from the top. Each number is a spin button read as 'Padding top, 16 pixels', and the link is a real toggle named 'Link all sides'. The box is 254px wide and narrows with its container (the number boxes go from 72px to 56px below 238px), down to about 200px, so it fits a small phone and an editor's inspector.

items.name: box-sides-field-demo
items.title: Box sides field demo
items.description: A working preview of Box sides field.

items.name: inline-field
items.title: Inline field
items.description: A checkbox, switch or radio with its label beside it, plus a description and an error beneath, wired together as one tap target.
items.docs: Put one Checkbox, Switch or RadioGroupItem inside it. InlineField gives the control its id, aria-describedby, aria-invalid, required and disabled, so the label, the description and the error are read in that order. The whole row is the click target, at least 44px high on a touch screen, the focus ring stays on the control, and a link in the label (terms, privacy) opens as a link without toggling the control. placement='end' pushes the control to the far edge, as a settings row does; invalid and disabled look the same on all three controls; a disabled row dims the control and its label and keeps the description at full strength, because that is where the reason goes.

items.name: inline-field-demo
items.title: Inline field demo
items.description: A working preview of Inline field.

items.name: choice-list
items.title: Choice list
items.description: One list for choosing one or several: label, description, media and a trailing value on every row, divided by hairlines, with an exclusive None row.
items.docs: mode='single' (the default) makes the rows radios and mode='multiple' makes them checkboxes; value and onValueChange are controlled or uncontrolled. Every row is a real control, so with a name a form submits name=value natively. Mark an option exclusive for 'None of these': choosing it clears the others and choosing any other clears it. media takes an icon or an avatar, trailing a price or a count, and a disabled option can say why in its description. A row without media keeps the room for it, so the labels stay in one line. A chosen row shows the control, a heavier label and a tint, never colour alone, and the count of picks is announced in multiple mode.

items.name: choice-list-demo
items.title: Choice list demo
items.description: A working preview of Choice list.

items.name: disabled-reason
items.title: Disabled reason
items.description: Say why a control is unavailable: it stays focusable with aria-disabled, shows the reason on hover, focus and tap, and refuses the click.
items.docs: Wrap one control and pass disabled and reason; do not also set disabled on the control. For a select or a menu wrap its trigger (SelectTrigger), not its root, which renders no element to refuse; the arrow keys and typing that would open or change it are refused too, and a refused Button does not dip on a press or change on hover. It sets aria-disabled instead of the native attribute, so the control stays in the tab order, is read as unavailable, and refuses the click, Enter and Space (a text field becomes read-only). The reason shows in a tooltip on hover, on focus and when the control is tapped, and is tied in with aria-describedby. inline prints it under the control, always or with 'touch' only where there is no hover; put the pair in a block or column container. With disabled false nothing is left behind, the markup is the control's own, and the control keeps its focus.

items.name: disabled-reason-demo
items.title: Disabled reason demo
items.description: A working preview of Disabled reason.

items.name: async-select
items.title: Async select
items.description: A select that asks your server as you type: debounced, with a loading row, a no-results line that repeats the query and stale answers dropped.
items.docs: loadOptions(query, signal) resolves with the options; pass the signal to fetch. Each new question aborts the one before it and a late answer is dropped, so an old answer can never replace a new one. value is the chosen option itself, so the field names it before anything has loaded. defaultOptions lists options before anything is typed (or true to ask the loader with an empty text), minChars and debounce set when it asks, and clearable adds a button that clears the choice and hands the focus to the field. A quick answer just swaps the list; a slow one shows a loading row. The list keeps one minimum height, so the loading row, the 'No results for acme' line and the error line with Retry never move anything under the input. messages replaces the words.

items.name: async-select-demo
items.title: Async select demo
items.description: A working preview of Async select.

items.name: creatable-select
items.title: Creatable select
items.description: Choose from a list or add a new entry: when nothing matches, a Create row appears as the last option, in single mode or as chips.
items.docs: onCreate(input) may be async and return the new option, or nothing to use the text itself. Enter takes the highlighted row, which is the Create row when it is all there is; Ctrl or Cmd with Enter always creates what was typed, and the Create row shows that shortcut when other rows are listed above it. While it runs, the Create row shows a spinner and the list cannot be touched; if it rejects, its message shows under the field and the typed text is kept. The new entry is chosen at once. normalise decides when two entries are the same (by default capitals and spaces at the ends do not count): a duplicate is never created, the existing one is chosen, and typing the name of something already chosen and pressing Enter says so instead of removing it. multiple turns the choice into removable chips, and Backspace in the empty search takes the last one back; taking a chip back with its own button leaves the focus on the next chip, else the one before it, else the field, and aria-invalid draws the destructive border around the whole chips field. messages replaces the words. Options have the shape of a Combobox option.

items.name: creatable-select-demo
items.title: Creatable select demo
items.description: A working preview of Creatable select.

items.name: language-select
items.title: Language select
items.description: Languages named in themselves and in your language, searchable by either name, with a short list of suggestions pinned on top.
items.docs: Only codes go in (languages, suggested) and one code comes out; there is no data to ship, because the names come from Intl.DisplayNames in the browser: the language in itself, large, and in locale, quietly beside it. The search ignores capitals and accents and reads the native name, the translated name, the code and the names in each locale of alsoSearch, so 'ger', 'deut' and, with alsoSearch={['en', 'fr']}, 'allem' all find German. A right-to-left name keeps its own direction inside the row while the layout stays left to right, every name carries lang so Chinese and Japanese get their own letterforms, and variants (pt-BR) sort next to their language. messages replaces the headings and the other words, so they can follow locale.

items.name: language-select-demo
items.title: Language select demo
items.description: A working preview of Language select.

items.name: chip-select
items.title: Chip select
items.description: Choose from a wrapping set of chips, one or several, with a check on the chosen ones, a minimum and maximum, and a spoken count that says why the rest turn off.
items.docs: mode="single" (the default) takes value as a string or null and reports the chip that was chosen; mode="multiple" takes and reports an array of values, always in the order of the chips. With max, the chips that are not chosen turn off once the limit is reached and the polite line under the chips says why ("Pick up to 5, 5 chosen"). With min the same line states the rule ("Pick at least 3"), and a shortfall turns into an error once the group has been left or a form with it is submitted: the browser's own bubble is cancelled, focus goes to the first chip and the line becomes the error. error shows a message from outside, labels.hint rewrites the line for another language, and name sends the choice with a plain form (one hidden input per value, or a radio in single mode). An icon is an element such as <IconStar />; a chosen chip swaps it for its check. Chips are 36px tall, with a 44px touch target on touch screens.

items.name: chip-select-demo
items.title: Chip select demo
items.description: A working preview of Chip select.

items.name: slider-field
items.title: Slider field
items.description: A slider with its label, live value in the right unit, end labels, a default marker with reset and an exact-value box.
items.docs: value, defaultValue and onValueChange work as on any field; defaultValue is also the default, so a tick on the track marks it and a Reset button, which only exists while the value is somewhere else, puts it back. formatValue writes the value in your unit and is used in the readout, at the ends and in aria-valuetext, so a screen reader hears "45 min". showInput adds a number field beside the track: it follows the slider and the slider follows it, what is typed is clamped and stepped (counted from min, like the slider) when you leave the field or press Enter, Escape takes it back and the arrow keys step. onValueCommit fires once when a drag or a key press settles, for a save that should not run on every pixel. marks takes numbers or { value, label }; a labelled mark at an end replaces the end label. name sends the value with a plain form, and labels changes the words of the buttons. locale (default en-US) decides how the number field reads what is typed and how it writes the value while you edit: with en-US "3,000" is three thousand and "1,5" one and a half, with nl-NL "3.000" is three thousand. A sign that is not the decimal one of the locale groups only when it stands alone with three digits after it, behind a number that does not start with a zero.

items.name: slider-field-demo
items.title: Slider field demo
items.description: A working preview of Slider field.

items.name: weekday-picker
items.title: Weekday picker
items.description: The days of the week as toggle chips: first day set by locale, weekday and weekend shortcuts and a spoken summary like Monday to Friday.
items.docs: value is a list of getDay() numbers, 0 for Sunday to 6 for Saturday, in any order; onValueChange reports them in ascending order. The row starts on weekStartsOn, by default the first day of the week in the locale (Sunday for en-US, Monday for en-GB and nl-NL). The names come from Intl.DateTimeFormat in the language of locale, so "M", "Mon" and "maandag" are all right, and every chip is named by the whole day. The sentence under the chips ("Monday to Friday", "Weekends", "Every day", "Tuesday and Thursday") and the preset labels exist in English, Dutch, German, French and Spanish; for another language pass labels. presets is true for Weekdays, Weekend and Every day, or a list mixing those keys with your own { label, days }; a preset is pressed while the choice equals it. With requireOne the last chosen day refuses to turn off and says why for a few seconds. name sends one hidden input per day.

items.name: weekday-picker-demo
items.title: Weekday picker demo
items.description: A working preview of Weekday picker.

items.name: async-switch
items.title: Async switch
items.description: A switch for settings that save at once: a spinner in the thumb while it waits, a rollback with a retry if the save fails, and the result read out.
items.docs: onCheckedChange(next) gets the position the switch is moving to. Return a promise and the switch waits for it: it moves at once, shows a spinner in the thumb, ignores further presses and says aria-busy; if the promise rejects, the thumb slides back and the message appears under the label with a Retry button, and if it resolves, Saved shows for successFor milliseconds (default 2000), in the row of the label so the description never narrows or wraps again (in a column narrower than 16rem it is the check alone, so a long label does not wrap either). Pass checked and update it in the handler once the save worked, or use defaultChecked and let the switch keep its own state the same way. A handler that returns nothing just changes the switch. status drives the display yourself, for example status={mutation.status}; Retry then calls onCheckedChange with the position that failed. successMessage, errorMessage and retryLabel change the words, which are read out politely. Under reduced motion the thumb jumps and the spinner is a still ellipsis.

items.name: async-switch-demo
items.title: Async switch demo
items.description: A working preview of Async switch.

items.name: likert-scale
items.title: Likert scale
items.description: Agree or disagree in five labelled steps: horizontal with a label under each step, a single column on a phone and one tab stop.
items.docs: value is the number of the chosen point, counted from 1, or "na" for the Not applicable choice, or null for no answer; onValueChange reports the number or "na". points (5 or 7) chooses the default labels, Strongly disagree to Strongly agree; options replaces them with your own, such as ["Never", "Rarely", "Sometimes", "Often", "Always"]. The layout follows the width of the container, not the screen: from 520px the points sit in a row on a line, below it they stack as a column of large targets. required makes the group aria-required and a form refuse to submit until a point is chosen; the missing answer shows as an error under the group (requiredMessage) once the group has been left or a submit was tried. error shows a message from outside. notApplicable adds a choice that stands apart, with your own words if you pass a string. name sends the number, or na, with a plain form.

items.name: likert-scale-demo
items.title: Likert scale demo
items.description: A working preview of Likert scale.

items.name: radio-table
items.title: Radio table
items.description: Compare while you choose: a radio per row, the specs in columns, a real table to a screen reader and cards on a phone.
items.docs: columns describe the table: the first column is the name of each choice and carries the radio, the others are the figures to compare, each with an optional align (start, center or end, the default), format (how the value is written) and speak (how it is read out). rows give a value, their cells by column key, an optional note under the name, and disabled: true, or a string that says why. To a screen reader it is a table with headers, and every radio is described by its row read in column order ("8 GB memory, 4 CPUs, 160 GB disk, 48 euros per month"); underneath the radios are real radio inputs that share one name, so there is one tab stop and the arrow keys move and choose. Where the container is narrower than 560px each row is a card with the heading beside each figure. name and required work as on any radio group in a form, and locale writes the numbers of columns without a format.

items.name: radio-table-demo
items.title: Radio table demo
items.description: A working preview of Radio table.

items.name: step-slider
items.title: Step slider
items.description: A slider that snaps to named steps such as Weekly, Monthly and Yearly, with labels under the track and the label spoken as the value.
items.docs: steps are { value, label, description? } in order, and the knob snaps to equally spaced stops whatever their number; value is the value of the chosen step. A screen reader hears the label and the place ("Monthly, 2 of 3") through aria-valuetext, the arrow keys move one stop, Home and End jump to the ends, and pressing a label chooses its stop. When the container is too narrow for every label (about 3.75rem for each) every other one steps aside, together with the two beside the chosen one, which always stays (with five stops an end label gives way beside the chosen one only below 17.5rem, a little later than the rest). The description of the chosen step shows under the track, and a polite live region reads it out; every description sits in one cell, so nothing moves when the knob does. showLabels={false} leaves the ticks alone and writes the chosen label beside the heading. name sends the chosen value with a plain form.

items.name: step-slider-demo
items.title: Step slider demo
items.description: A working preview of Step slider.

items.name: listbox
items.title: Listbox
items.description: An always-open list to choose from: one or several with Shift ranges, grouped options with descriptions, typeahead and an optional search.
items.docs: options are { value, label, description, icon, disabled, group }; options with the same group are shown together under one sticky heading. The list is one tab stop and keeps the focus on itself (or on the search field when searchable), pointing at the active option with aria-activedescendant. Arrow keys move, Home and End go to the ends, typing jumps to the next option that starts with it, Enter and Space choose. With selectionMode="multiple", Space toggles, Shift with the arrows or a click chooses the range from the anchor, Control or Command with A chooses every option (from the search field only while it is empty), and a live line reads "N selected". searchable adds a search field above the list: every word typed must be in the label or the description, ignoring case and accents, the matches are marked, the arrow keys and Enter work from inside the field and Escape clears it. Pressing an option never moves the focus into the field: with a mouse the field keeps the focus if it has it, and otherwise (always on a touch screen) the list takes it, so a tap does not raise the on-screen keyboard. height is the tallest the list grows before it scrolls inside its box. name sends the chosen values with a plain form.

items.name: listbox-demo
items.title: Listbox demo
items.description: A working preview of Listbox.

items.name: expiry-select
items.title: Expiry select
items.description: Choose how long something lasts: presets such as 7 days, 30 days or never, a custom date, and the resulting date written out under the field.
items.docs: value is an absolute calendar date such as "2026-12-02", or null for never, so what is stored cannot drift with the clock; onValueChange reports the date a choice comes to. presets are { label, days } counted from from (a date, a Date or a timestamp; default now, in timeZone, default UTC). A preset that would end after max (a date) is turned off and says where the limit is, and Custom date opens the house date picker, limited to between the start and max. The line under the field writes the date out ("Expires Tue 17 Nov 2026") or says "Never expires"; a date that has passed, or lies beyond max, marks the field invalid and says so there. allowNever adds the Never choice. The server render writes nothing that depends on the clock, so nothing mismatches. name sends the date, or never. labels changes the words, and locale the language the dates are written in (default en-US; en-GB writes "Tue 17 Nov 2026").

items.name: expiry-select-demo
items.title: Expiry select demo
items.description: A working preview of Expiry select.

items.name: emoji-scale
items.title: Emoji scale
items.description: Five faces from awful to great as a real radio group, named for screen readers, with a quiet pop when chosen and no colour to tell them apart.
items.docs: value is the number of the chosen face, 1 (awful) to 5 (great), or null for none; onValueChange reports the number. labels replaces the five words, worst first, and each one names its face for assistive technology: a screen reader hears "Good, 4 of 5". The faces differ in shape and not in colour (squeezed eyes and a deep frown, a small frown, a flat mouth, a small smile, laughing eyes over an open smile), so they read in monochrome and for colour-blind people. The chosen face fills its disc and grows a little, which is skipped under reduced motion. Pointing at or focusing a face writes its word under the row in a quieter weight without choosing it; showLabels={false} leaves that line out and the words stay in the accessible names. The chosen word is announced politely. size is sm, md or lg (24, 32 or 40px faces); every face sits in a target of 44px or more, and on a narrow screen the faces close up instead of running off the side. name sends the number with a plain form, and required marks the group.

items.name: emoji-scale-demo
items.title: Emoji scale demo
items.description: A working preview of Emoji scale.

items.name: multi-date-picker
items.title: Multi date picker
items.description: Pick several separate days on one calendar: click to add, Shift-click for a run, a chip list underneath and a limit if you want one.
items.docs: value is a list of ISO dates ("2026-10-27") in any order; onValueChange reports them in date order, each once. A click adds a day or takes it away, and Shift-click adds every day between the last pick and this one (days that cannot be picked are left out). The keyboard works as in the house Calendar: arrows move by day and week, Page Up and Down by month (Shift for a year), Home and End to the ends of the week, Enter or Space picks, and Shift with them adds a run. min and max bound the days that can be picked, disabledDates takes a list or a function for holidays and sold-out days, and a day that is out of reach is struck through inside its month. maxDates sets a limit: once it is reached the days that are not picked turn off and carry the reason (aria-describedby points at it), and a run that does not fit is cut short from the last pick outwards, with a line that says how many days were added. The chosen days are listed as removable chips with the weekday ("Tue 27 Oct", with the year added when the picks span years); Backspace or Delete on a chip's remove button hands the focus to the chip beside it. One polite line counts the picks ("3 dates selected, up to 5"), and Clear removes everything in one step. locale names the weekdays and months, weekStartsOn sets the first column, timeZone only decides which day is today, defaultMonth sets where an empty picker opens, and labels replaces every sentence. name sends one hidden input per day.

items.name: multi-date-picker-demo
items.title: Multi date picker demo
items.description: A working preview of Multi date picker.

items.name: repeat-select
items.title: Repeat select
items.description: Repeat options worked out from the start date (Every week on Tuesday, Every month on the 27th) that return a ready-to-use RRULE string.
items.docs: start is the first day, as an ISO date; the weekday, the day of the month and the month in the labels come from it, written by Intl in the locale you pass. value is the recurrence rule as a calendar file writes it ("RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=TU"), or null for no repeat; onValueChange reports the new rule. The choices are Does not repeat, Every day, Every week on Tuesday, Every month on the 27th (in the last seven days of a month it reads "on the last Tuesday" and becomes BYDAY=-1TU), Every year on 27 October and Every weekday (Monday to Friday); include picks which of them to offer, and they always keep that order. When start changes, the rule moves with it: a weekly rule on Tuesday becomes one on Thursday, the labels change together with it, onValueChange is called with the new rule and the change is announced. A rule that none of the choices describes (every other week, a count, an end date) shows as Custom with the rule under it; onCustom adds a Custom choice that hands the current rule to your own editor. Rules are read in any equivalent spelling, so FREQ=WEEKLY on a Tuesday is the weekly choice. labels replaces every sentence, for another language, and the helpers in repeat-select/rules.ts (ruleFor, kindOf) work without the component. name sends the rule with a plain form.

items.name: repeat-select-demo
items.title: Repeat select demo
items.description: A working preview of Repeat select.

items.name: histogram-slider
items.title: Histogram slider
items.description: A range slider over a distribution: bars drawn in CSS behind the track fade outside the chosen range, with minimum and maximum fields.
items.docs: buckets are the counts of equal parts of the range, from min to max, one bar each. The bars are drawn in CSS behind the track, full strength inside the chosen range and faint outside, cut exactly at the handles, and hidden from assistive technology. The sentence under the heading ("312 homes between 800 and 1,400 euros") carries the information and is read out politely as the handles move: noun gives the singular and plural of what is counted, formatValue writes a value, and summary writes the whole sentence if you say it differently. The count is exact when the handles stand on the edges of the bars and an estimate between them. value and onValueChange work as on any field with a [low, high] pair; onValueCommit fires once when a drag ends or a key press settles. The handles never cross, so the minimum cannot pass the maximum. Each is a slider with a 44px target and takes the arrow keys, the Page keys (ten steps), Home and End; a press anywhere on the track moves the nearest one, and handles that stand together are told apart by the way the pointer goes. The minimum and maximum fields stay in step with the handles, are clamped between the limits and the other end, and read numbers the way the locale writes them ("1,400" or "1.400").

items.name: histogram-slider-demo
items.title: Histogram slider demo
items.description: A working preview of Histogram slider.

items.name: threshold-slider
items.title: Threshold slider
items.description: Set warning and critical levels on one track: two handles divide it into OK, Warning and Critical zones, named in words and shown by pattern.
items.docs: value is { warn, critical }: the warning starts at warn and the critical zone at critical, with OK below. min, max and step set the scale, unit is written after the numbers (a symbol such as % sticks to the number, a word such as ms stands apart) and zoneLabels renames OK, Warning and Critical. The handles never cross and never come closer than minGap (one step by default). Each is a slider with a 44px target and a spoken value that says the zone it opens ("Warning starts at 70 percent"; spokenUnit changes the word for the unit). The zones are told apart by tone, pattern and name: plain, hatched and dotted, so they read in monochrome and for colour-blind people. A scale under the bar shows the ends and both levels in tabular figures, and a number that would touch its neighbour makes way. The legend names and measures each zone ("OK to 70%, Warning 70 to 90%, Critical above 90%"), and each handle has its own number field, clamped between the other handle and the limits. Arrow keys move one step, Shift or the Page keys ten, Home and End go to the limits, and a press on the bar moves the nearest handle. onValueCommit fires once when a drag or a key press settles.

items.name: threshold-slider-demo
items.title: Threshold slider demo
items.description: A working preview of Threshold slider.

items.name: allocation-slider
items.title: Allocation slider
items.description: Split 100% between parts: draggable dividers on one bar, a number field per part, a lockable part and a total that must read 100.
items.docs: parts are { id, label } in the order they stand on the bar, and value is a record of what each holds, by id; onValueChange reports the whole record. total (default 100), step and min (the least any part may hold) set the rules, and unit is written after the numbers. The dividers between the parts are sliders in their own right: dragging one moves the share between the part on its left and the part on its right, so the total stays fixed, and its spoken value names both ("Email 40%, Social 35%"). Arrow keys move a step, Shift or the Page keys ten, Home and End to the least either part can hold. Each part also has a number field: typing a share takes the difference from the other free parts, or gives it to them, in proportion to what they hold, and the number is kept to what they can make room for. With lockable every part gets a lock. A locked part keeps its share, its field is read-only, and the dividers on its sides slide along with it while the free parts on either side trade between themselves (locked and defaultLocked, with onLockedChange, set the locks). The readout at the top says "Adds up to 100%", or what is missing or too much, and Balance spreads that over the free parts; data that does not add up shows its unassigned part in the bar. Parts are told apart by name and by a shade of grey, never by colour alone. Several dividers that stand on one spot (a part with nothing in it) are told apart by the way the pointer goes. The helpers in allocation-slider/shares.ts (evenShares, setShare, balance) work without the component.

items.name: preview-picker
items.title: Preview picker
items.description: Choose from a list while a preview of the highlighted option sits beside it: templates, email layouts, themes, export formats.
items.docs: options are { value, label, description?, preview?, disabled? } and the list on the left is a radio group: Tab enters it once; the arrow keys, Home and End move the focus and so preview an option without choosing it; Space, Enter or a click chooses. Pointing at an option previews it as well, and the preview goes back to the chosen one when the pointer leaves. renderPreview(option) draws the preview of the option being previewed; an option can also carry a ready preview node, which can come from a server component. The pane is a labelled region (previewLabel names it), keeps one shape for every option (previewClassName sets it, 4 by 3 by default) so the layout does not jump, never takes the focus, and says in a polite line which option is previewed and which is chosen ("Previewing Minimal, current choice: Classic"). The layout follows the width of the container, not the screen: from 720px the preview sits beside the list, and below it the preview moves under the list behind a Show preview button. A disabled option is skipped by the arrow keys. labels replaces the sentence and the two button names. name sends the chosen value with a plain form.

items.title: Preview picker demo

items.name: cascade-select
items.title: Cascade select
items.description: Pick a path through a hierarchy: columns that open to the right on desktop, a drill-down list on a phone and the full path in the field.
items.docs: options are { value, label, children?, disabled? } and the value is the path of values, one for each step (value, defaultValue, onValueChange). With changeOnSelect a choice that opens more can be the answer too, and a click picks it and opens it. On a screen wide enough for every level (14rem each) the panel shows one column per open level: Right opens a choice and moves into it, Left goes back, Up, Down, Home and End move in a column, Enter or Space picks, and Escape closes. Below that width the same panel is a drill-down list with a back row ("Back to Electronics") and the path above the list, and it opens at the level of the chosen choice. The field shows the whole path (separator sets what stands between the steps), with the front given up first when it is too long so the last step is read (when less than about three characters of the front would be left, it goes altogether, separator included, and the last step stands alone), and the full path as its tooltip. The search box flattens the tree to the paths that hold every word you type, ignoring case and accents, with the match in strong type; typing a letter on a choice sends it to the search, the first Escape empties it and Enter picks the first match. The columns are a tree, so every choice has aria-level, aria-setsize, aria-posinset and, when it opens more, aria-expanded and a spoken count of the choices inside it, and the depth you reach is announced; the matches of a search are a plain listbox. defaultOpen starts the panel open for a preview, and labels replaces every sentence. name sends the values of the path joined with a slash.

items.title: Cascade select demo

items.name: icon-picker
items.title: Icon picker
items.description: Choose an icon for a project or a list: a searchable grid of the icons you pass in, arrow keys in two directions and every name spoken.
items.docs: icons is a record of name to icon, each icon a rendered element ({ folder: <IconFolder />, rocket: <IconRocket /> }), so the same set can be passed from a Server Component and from a client module. value is the name of the chosen icon, or null, and onValueChange reports the name; the None cell, switched on with allowNone, reports null. labels gives each icon a name for people ({ rocket: "Rocket launch" }): it is what the search reads and what a screen reader says for the cell, and icons without one are named from their key. keywords adds words the search also finds an icon by. The search matches every word of the query in any order, ignores case and accents, and Enter chooses the first match. The grid is one tab stop: the arrow keys move in two dimensions, Home and End go to the ends of a row (with Ctrl, of the grid), Page Up and Page Down move by rows, and typing a letter on the grid moves to the search. columns is the most icons in a row (6 by default, fewer on a narrow screen); cells are 40px with a 44px target, and the grid scrolls inside the popover without moving the page. The popover keeps 12px from every edge of the screen and, on a short screen, shrinks to the room it has, so the search is always within reach. Name the field with aria-labelledby (the id of a visible label) or aria-label: the name of the chosen icon is added to it, so a screen reader hears the label and the choice together and voice control can say "click Rocket". messages replaces every sentence, name sends the chosen name with a plain form, and open, defaultOpen and onOpenChange control the popover.

items.name: rank-list
items.title: Rank list
items.description: Put things in order: drag a row, or press Space and use the arrows, with the new position announced and numbers that follow the move.
items.docs: items are the things to rank (an id, a label and an optional description); value is the ids in rank order and onValueChange reports the whole new order once, when a row is dropped, never during the drag. Each row has a grip for the mouse, a pen and a finger, and answers to the keyboard: Space or Enter picks a row up, Up and Down move it (Home and End go to the ends), Space or Enter drops it and Escape puts it back, with every step announced politely ("Moved to position 2 of 5"). moveButtons adds Move up and Move down buttons to each row, for people and devices that cannot drag. numbered shows each rank in tabular figures and renumbers it live as a row passes. The lifted row gets a fine outline instead of a shadow while the others make room, nothing animates under reduced motion, and a list given a maxHeight scrolls itself while a row is dragged near its edge (so does the page). name sends the ids, in order, with a plain form; messages replaces every sentence.

items.name: shortcut-recorder
items.title: Shortcut recorder
items.description: A field that records a key combination: press the keys and see them as keycaps; Escape cancels, Backspace clears and conflicts are named.
items.docs: value is a combination written the same on every platform, Mod+Shift+K, where Mod is Command on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere; onValueChange reports the new one, or null when it is cleared. Focusing the field starts recording: the held modifiers show live as keycaps, and the combination is committed when a key that is not a modifier lands. Escape cancels, Backspace or Delete clears, and Tab always moves on, so the field never traps focus; a reminder under the field says so while it records. reserved is a list of combinations that cannot be used, or an object that gives the reason for each; findConflict is given a combination and returns the name of what already uses it. Either one refuses the combination with the reason in words ("Already used by Search"), and requireModifier also refuses a key pressed alone, naming keys the shown keyboard has (needsModifier in messages can be a function of the platform). platform shows the keys of a Mac (⌘ ⇧ ⌥) or of Windows and Linux (Ctrl Shift Alt), and by default is read from the browser after mount. A screen reader hears the shortcut as words ("Command plus Shift plus K"). While it has focus the field listens at the top of the window, so a dialog around it does not close on the Escape that cancels a recording. messages replaces every sentence, and name sends the combination with a plain form.

items.title: Shortcut recorder demo
items.description: A working preview of Shortcut recorder.

items.name: container
items.title: Container
items.description: The page-width wrapper: a centred column with fluid gutters, five named widths and room for the notch.
items.docs: size is narrow (40rem), prose (46rem), default (72rem), wide (88rem) or full (no limit), and counts the gutters. The gutters are fluid, 16px on a phone growing to 32px on a desktop, and they add the safe-area inset, so content stays clear of a notch in landscape (the larger of the left and right inset on both sides, so the column stays centred). padded={false} turns the gutters off, for a Container inside another Container: it then only caps the width, so the padding never doubles. as renders main, section, header, footer, nav, article or aside instead of a div, which gives a page its landmarks without an extra wrapper. The gutter is available to anything inside as --container-gutter.

items.name: container-demo
items.title: Container demo
items.description: A working preview of Container.

items.name: form-grid
items.title: Form grid
items.description: A form layout on a 12-column grid: fields span columns, wrap predictably and stack at 320px with their hints aligned.
items.docs: FormGrid is a grid of columns (12 by default) and FormGrid.Item puts one field in it. span is the number of columns, as a number or as an object per width ({ base: 12, sm: 6, lg: 4 }); a plain number applies from the sm width up and below it the field takes the whole row, so a form stacks on a narrow screen by itself. start leaves room in front of an item, and fullWidth takes the whole row at every width. The widths are those of the grid itself, not of the window (sm from 28rem, md from 36rem, lg from 48rem), so the same form behaves the same in a page, a dialog and a sheet. Items align to the top, so a hint or an error under one field never pushes its neighbour out of line, and the DOM order is the reading order at every width. as="fieldset" with a legend groups the fields, and disabled switches them all off together. gap is sm, md or lg.

items.title: Form grid demo
items.description: A working preview of Form grid.

items.name: section-shell
items.title: Section shell
items.description: A titled page section: heading, description, actions and content in one landmark, with the spacing and anchor already right.
items.docs: title names the section and the section is labelled by it, so it shows up in a screen reader's list of landmarks; level is h2 to h4. description sits under the title and actions on its line, where they wrap beneath it on a phone. tone is plain (a hairline under the header), bordered (a card with a ruled header and footer) or muted (a soft panel). footer is a row under the content, and empty is what to show when there are no children, so a section never shows a lonely heading. id makes the section a link target, with a scroll margin of --section-scroll-offset (5rem) so a sticky header never covers its heading. Stacked sections keep a gap of --section-shell-gap (2rem) between them, with no margin at the call site.
